cards.title: ICC Enforcement in the Philippines Becomes a Test of Domestic Sovereignty vs International Accountability
cards.background: Ronald Dela Rosa, a Philippine senator and former police chief who oversaw Rodrigo Duterte's anti-drug campaign, took refuge inside the Philippine Senate hours before the International Criminal Court unsealed a warrant for his arrest. He is accused of being an indirect co-perpetrator in killings of at least 32 people between 2016 and 2018, while Duterte himself has been in ICC custody in The Hague since March 2025. The Philippine police said they would not arrest Dela Rosa while he remained under Senate custody, and his lawyers have asked the Supreme Court to block any arrest without a Philippine judicial warrant. The case comes amid a wider Duterte-Marcos feud, with the lower house voting to impeach Vice-President Sara Duterte on the same day the Senate elected a new president.

prop_args.thesis: Allowing ICC enforcement against powerful domestic actors is necessary to end impunity and make mass atrocity law credible.
mechanisms: First, ICC action breaks the protection racket that domestic elites build around themselves. This is because (1) local police and courts are often captured by the same political networks that ordered or tolerated abuses, (2) senior officials can hide behind procedural delays and jurisdictional disputes, and (3) arrest warrants create a concrete enforcement point that domestic victims cannot generate on their own.

Second, international prosecution deters future abuse by raising the personal cost for commanders, not just foot soldiers. Three reasons: one, it signals that political office does not erase liability; two, it forces mid-level enforcers to think twice before carrying out unlawful campaigns; three, it weakens the norm that mass killings are an acceptable tool of governance.

Third, this strengthens long-term state legitimacy and transitional justice. This matters because (1) victims get acknowledgment that the state failed them, (2) future governments inherit a cleaner institutional baseline, and (3) democratic competition becomes less distorted when candidates cannot rely on violent patronage networks to stay untouchable.

opp_args.thesis: ICC intervention can backfire by turning accountability into a sovereignty crisis that hardens domestic resistance and politicizes justice.
mechanisms: First, external enforcement can trigger nationalist backlash that protects the accused. One, elites can frame the ICC as foreign interference, which is especially potent when the accused claims local courts should decide; two, that narrative mobilizes supporters around sovereignty rather than the underlying crimes; three, it makes cooperation with international institutions politically costly for domestic officials.

Second, selective or delayed international justice can deepen polarization instead of healing it. One, when prosecutions arrive years later, they are easily read as revenge by rival factions; two, if one camp is targeted while allies escape, the process looks partisan; three, that perception can undermine trust in both the ICC and domestic institutions.

Third, weak enforcement capacity means warrants may produce spectacle without real accountability. One, if suspects can shelter in legislatures or rely on procedural shields, the ICC cannot compel compliance on its own; two, failed arrests can embolden other perpetrators by showing the limits of international law; three, the gap between legal principle and actual enforcement can reduce deterrence rather than increase it.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether international prosecution actually changes behavior or merely creates symbolic confrontation. Prop wins if the round is about ending entrenched impunity; opp wins if the focus is on backlash, selectivity, and the limits of enforcement in a sovereign state with divided institutions.

cards.title: India’s Gold Demand Shock Exposes How Fast Household Savings Can Be Redirected
cards.background: Bloomberg reports that India’s top jeweler expects only a brief slowdown if gold buying is curbed. The article notes that gold prices have risen nearly 60% this year to record highs, yet demand remains strong in India, China, and Turkey because buyers expect current prices to look cheap in a few months. The photo context places the story in Mumbai’s Zaveri Bazaar ahead of Dhanteras, a major gold-buying festival in India.

prop_args.thesis: Curbing gold buying would be a useful short-term policy because it can redirect household savings from unproductive hoarding into more productive financial assets and consumption.
mechanisms: First, restricting or discouraging gold purchases shifts savings into the formal financial system. This is because (1) gold is a low-yield store of value, (2) households often treat it as dead capital rather than investable capital, and (3) moving even a portion of that demand into deposits, bonds, or mutual funds increases credit available for firms and households.

Second, a curb can reduce external vulnerability. Three reasons: one, India imports large volumes of gold, so demand directly worsens the trade balance; two, lower import demand reduces pressure on the current account and the rupee; three, less import-led outflow gives policymakers more room to stabilize inflation and foreign exchange reserves.

Third, the policy can be defended as a temporary demand-management tool rather than a permanent cultural ban. This matters because if gold buying is being driven by a speculative rush after a nearly 60% price surge, then even a brief slowdown can break momentum, cool panic buying, and prevent households from chasing an asset at peak prices.

opp_args.thesis: Trying to curb gold buying is economically and politically counterproductive because it attacks a deeply embedded household savings behavior without solving the underlying reasons people buy gold.
mechanisms: First, gold demand is a hedge against distrust in financial institutions and macro instability. One, many households prefer a tangible asset they understand; two, gold protects against inflation, currency depreciation, and banking risk; three, if the state suppresses gold demand, savers may simply shift into other informal or unproductive assets rather than into productive finance.

Second, the policy risks hurting a major retail and jewelry ecosystem. One, India’s jewelry sector depends on festival-driven demand like Dhanteras and wedding-season purchases; two, a curbed market would reduce sales, employment, and working capital for small traders; three, because the article itself says the slowdown would be brief, the economic pain may be immediate while the macro gains are limited.

Third, gold is not just speculation but a culturally and financially rational savings vehicle for many households. One, families use it for intergenerational wealth storage and emergency liquidity; two, in the absence of universal access to trusted financial products, gold serves as a private insurance mechanism; three, coercive curbs can therefore be regressive, disproportionately affecting middle- and lower-income savers rather than wealthy investors.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether gold demand is treated as wasted capital or as a rational hedge in a low-trust economy. Prop wins if the judge prioritizes macro efficiency and external stability; opp wins if they emphasize household autonomy and the limits of state capacity to re-engineer savings behavior.

THBT governments should discourage investment in non-productive stores of value
THP a world where major economies tax or restrict gold purchases to redirect savings into formal finance

cards.title: Israel’s 7 October Death-Penalty Tribunal Trades Due Process for Retributive Sovereignty
cards.background: Israel’s Knesset passed a new law by 93 votes to 0 creating a special legal framework for prosecuting people alleged to have directly participated in the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attacks and hostage-taking. The law allows for the death penalty and public trials, including filmed opening, verdict, and sentencing hearings broadcast on a dedicated website, and applies to suspects such as members of Hamas’s Nukhba unit captured in Israel. Human rights groups warn the framework may rely on confessions extracted under torture and weaken ordinary criminal safeguards, while supporters frame it as a historic accountability process comparable to the Eichmann trial.

prop_args.thesis: Israel should create a special tribunal with capital punishment and public proceedings for 7 October perpetrators because mass atrocity crimes require exceptional accountability that ordinary criminal law cannot deliver.
mechanisms: First, the special tribunal restores deterrence and state credibility after an unprecedented mass-casualty attack. This is because (1) the 7 October assault killed over 1,200 people and involved 251 hostages, so the scale is far beyond ordinary terrorism cases, (2) a bespoke framework signals that mass murder and sexual violence against civilians will trigger the maximum legal response, and (3) public sentencing creates a visible state monopoly on punishment that can reassure a traumatized public and deter copycat atrocities.

Second, a tailored court is necessary to process an unusually large and complex evidentiary record. Three reasons: one, investigators reportedly reviewed thousands of hours of video and audio plus interrogation material, two, the defendants are alleged to be part of a coordinated military-terror structure rather than isolated offenders, and three, a special military court can adapt procedure to handle classified intelligence, mass victim testimony, and cross-border evidence without collapsing under standard criminal rules.

Third, public trials serve a truth-telling and victim-healing function that private proceedings cannot. This matters because (1) many families still lack answers about killings and hostage deaths, (2) broadcasting key moments can create a shared historical record and deny perpetrators the ability to hide behind secrecy, and (3) for societies facing atrocity, formal public condemnation can be as important as punishment in restoring moral order and preventing denial.

opp_args.thesis: Israel should not use a death-penalty special tribunal because it undermines due process, risks wrongful convictions, and turns justice into political theater.
mechanisms: First, the framework weakens evidentiary safeguards and increases the chance of executing the wrong people. One, human rights groups say some detainees have been tortured and that confessions may be coerced, two, the law contemplates hearings where defendants may not even be physically present, and three, once the state lowers procedural protections in a politically charged mass case, the risk of irreversible error becomes unacceptable because death penalty cases cannot be corrected after execution.

Second, public trials and a special military court incentivize show-trial dynamics rather than neutral adjudication. One, the law was explicitly sold as a spectacle with filmed openings, verdicts, and sentencing, two, coalition politicians have framed it in openly retributive language about making victims look into the eyes of 'murderers, rapists and kidnappers,' and three, that political pressure makes judges more likely to confirm pre-decided outcomes than independently test evidence.

Third, the law may damage Israel’s international legitimacy and fuel further conflict rather than closure. One, capital punishment is highly controversial and Israel has long been de facto abolitionist, two, executing Palestinians after a mass war will be read by many actors as collective punishment rather than individualized justice, and three, that perception can deepen radicalization, complicate hostage diplomacy, and give Israel’s critics a powerful propaganda tool.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is between expressive justice and irreversible legal error. Prop wins if the round is about exceptional atrocity and state legitimacy; opp wins if the judge prioritizes due process, because once the state executes someone, any procedural abuse or mistaken conviction is permanent.

cards.title: China’s Food and Fertiliser Stockpiling Turns Global Supply Shocks Into a Geopolitical Weapon
cards.background: Former World Bank president David Malpass told the BBC that China should stop hoarding food and fertiliser as global markets face a supply crunch linked to the Iran war and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. China has halted exports of several types of fertiliser since March, citing domestic supply protection, on top of restrictions that have been in place since 2021. The article says China accounted for around 25% of global fertiliser output last year, with exports totalling more than $13bn, and that nations are now scrambling to secure fertiliser ahead of spring planting.

prop_args.thesis: China should release fertiliser and food stocks because its export restrictions are amplifying a global food-security shock and raising the cost of instability for import-dependent states.
mechanisms: First, releasing stockpiles reduces immediate price spikes in a market with very inelastic short-run supply. This is because (1) farmers need fertiliser before planting deadlines, so they cannot wait for new capacity, (2) China is a major producer at roughly 25% of global fertiliser output, so even modest export changes move world prices, and (3) the article notes exports were already worth more than $13bn, showing the scale of trade being withheld.

Second, China’s hoarding behavior worsens the distributional impact of the Iran-related shipping shock. Three reasons: one, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz already disrupts shipments, two, export bans force poorer importers to bid against richer buyers and lose access, and three, food and fertiliser are politically sensitive inputs, so shortages translate quickly into inflation, unrest, and government legitimacy crises in vulnerable states.

Third, China gains more from being seen as a stabilizer than from extracting short-term strategic leverage. This matters because (1) China benefits from open waterways and global trade flows, (2) it runs shipping lines and owns containers, so it has a systemic interest in predictable commerce, and (3) acting as a supplier of last resort would improve its diplomatic standing while reducing accusations that it is weaponizing interdependence.

opp_args.thesis: China is justified in restricting fertiliser and food exports because domestic supply security and price stability take priority during a wartime global shock.
mechanisms: First, export controls protect domestic consumers and farmers from external volatility. One, if the Strait of Hormuz disruption raises import costs, China risks transmitting global scarcity into its own food system, two, fertiliser is a strategic input for agricultural output, and three, governments are politically punished far more for domestic food inflation than for foreign criticism.

Second, China can argue it is responding to a genuine supply emergency rather than acting as a pure spoiler. One, the article says the root cause is the Iran war and shipping disruption, two, China had already faced restrictions since 2021, suggesting a longer-term supply management policy, and three, in a crisis states often prioritize national resilience over global market efficiency.

Third, the developing-country framing gives China legal and normative cover to preserve policy space. One, Beijing can claim it remains the largest developing country and therefore deserves flexibility in WTO-style obligations, two, that status helps justify industrial and food-security protections, and three, forcing China to behave like a fully liberalized rich economy without reciprocal obligations would be politically unsustainable domestically.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether China is a stabilizing supplier or a crisis amplifier in a market where timing matters more than long-run capacity. Prop wins if the round is about immediate food-security harms and global spillovers; opp wins if the judge prioritizes sovereign resilience and accepts that states facing external shocks may legitimately hoard strategic inputs.

cards.title: Escalating Israeli Strikes Trap Southern Lebanese Civilians Between Displacement and Deterrence
cards.background: On 12 May 2026, Al Jazeera reported from southern Lebanon that residents displaced by Israeli strikes say they will not flee again despite a sharp rise in deaths and intensifying attacks. The report frames a renewed cycle of violence in areas near the Israel-Lebanon border, where civilians who previously left their homes are now weighing the costs of displacement against the risks of staying. The article does not provide exact casualty totals, but it explicitly notes escalating strikes and increasing fatalities in the south.

prop_args.thesis: Escalating strikes and repeated displacement will harden Lebanese civilian resistance while deepening the humanitarian and political costs for Israel and its local objectives.
mechanisms: First, repeated displacement creates a 'no more to lose' effect among civilians. This is because (1) people who have already been uprooted once are less responsive to further coercion, (2) staying becomes a form of defiance that preserves dignity and community ties, and (3) the population becomes harder to move, so military pressure stops translating into strategic leverage.

Second, intensified strikes increase civilian casualties and international backlash. Three reasons: one, higher death tolls generate stronger media attention and NGO documentation, two, images of civilians refusing to flee despite bombardment sharpen the asymmetry narrative, and three, this raises diplomatic costs for Israel by increasing pressure from allies, UN bodies, and humanitarian actors.

Third, the cycle of destruction undermines long-term security by entrenching grievance and recruitment. This matters because (1) destroyed homes and repeated trauma create durable resentment, (2) armed groups can exploit the perception that civilians are abandoned or collectively punished, and (3) even if immediate military targets are hit, the conflict becomes more entrenched and harder to de-escalate.

opp_args.thesis: Escalating strikes can still achieve deterrence and degrade hostile infrastructure, even if some civilians refuse to leave.
mechanisms: First, military pressure can impose real operational costs on armed actors. One, strikes disrupt logistics, command nodes, and mobility; two, the threat of continued escalation forces adversaries to divert resources into defense and concealment; three, even partial displacement can reduce the density of support networks available to militants.

Second, civilian refusal to flee does not negate strategic effects. One, many people staying in place may be unable to relocate rather than choosing to resist; two, the presence of civilians can constrain militant movement and make it harder to embed in populated areas; three, if the goal is deterrence, visible damage can still signal that cross-border escalation carries a high price.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether coercive pressure changes behavior faster than it creates backlash. Prop wins if the key metric is long-term stability and civilian protection; opp wins if the key metric is immediate deterrence and degrading hostile capability. The structural advantage usually lies with prop because repeated displacement and civilian harm are easier to document than any uncertain military gain.

cards.title: Morales Arrest Warrant Risks Turning Bolivia’s Rule-of-Law Case Into Nationwide Political Violence
cards.background: A Bolivian judge reissued an arrest warrant for former president Evo Morales on 12 May 2026 after he failed to appear for the start of his trial in Tarija on charges of trafficking a minor. Morales, who governed Bolivia from 2006 to 2019, is accused of fathering a child with a 15-year-old girl while in office; prosecutors say his absence confirms fugitive status and have also sought a travel ban. Morales has been sheltering since late 2024 in Chapare, his coca-growing stronghold, where supporters previously blocked roads for 24 days in October 2024 to stop police from reaching him.

prop_args.thesis: Enforcing the warrant is necessary to restore judicial credibility and prevent Bolivia’s political elite from becoming permanently above the law.
mechanisms: First, arresting Morales reasserts that even the most powerful ex-presidents can be prosecuted. This is because (1) selective impunity is what destroys trust in courts, (2) a visible enforcement action signals that political status does not override criminal liability, and (3) it deters future leaders from using office, loyalist networks, or rural strongholds to evade justice.

Second, the state has to act or it normalizes parallel sovereignty in Chapare. Three reasons: one, Morales is being sheltered by armed or organized supporters who have already blocked roads for 24 days, two, allowing a former president to remain untouchable in a protected enclave encourages other factions to build their own coercive bases, and three, the government’s inability to execute warrants would weaken the monopoly on force and embolden broader lawlessness.

Third, the case is politically costly but institutionally necessary because accountability for alleged abuse of power has long-run legitimacy benefits. This matters because (1) Bolivia’s democratic order is already scarred by Morales’s 2019 exit and fraud-tainted elections, (2) failing to prosecute serious allegations involving a minor would deepen cynicism about elite capture, and (3) a functioning state must sometimes absorb short-term unrest to prevent a culture of permanent exception for powerful actors.

opp_args.thesis: Pushing ahead with Morales’s arrest now is likely to trigger destabilization that outweighs any immediate rule-of-law gains.
mechanisms: First, the arrest attempt can become a mass-mobilization trigger in Morales’s strongholds. One, supporters have already threatened an 'insurgency across Bolivia,' two, Chapare has a history of organized road blockades that can paralyze transport and commerce, and three, the state may lack the capacity to arrest him without escalating into violent clashes.

Second, the prosecution may be perceived as politically selective, which undermines legitimacy rather than strengthening it. One, Morales is a polarizing ex-president who retains a large Indigenous and rural base, two, his lawyers argue he was not properly notified and that summons were served by edict, and three, if the public sees the case as elite revenge after his 2019 ouster, the trial can harden polarization and weaken confidence in institutions.

Third, the government risks creating a martyr whose arrest strengthens the very movement it wants to weaken. One, Morales remains a symbolic figure for anti-elite politics and Indigenous representation, two, coercive action against him can unify fragmented opposition networks around a common grievance, and three, once the issue becomes 'defend Evo' rather than 'answer the charges,' the state loses control of the political agenda.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is between institutional legitimacy and immediate stability. Prop wins if you think a state that cannot enforce warrants against powerful ex-leaders is already hollowing out; opp wins if you think enforcement will trigger a coercive backlash that the Bolivian state cannot contain.

cards.title: Australia’s Budget Turns Housing Tax Reform Into a Bid to Defuse Populist Backlash
cards.background: Ahead of the 2026 federal budget, Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the government would respond to economic anxieties that are “driving” Australians toward One Nation and other right-wing populist parties. Labor and Anthony Albanese have signaled major changes to negative gearing, capital gains tax, and trusts, alongside measures to improve housing supply and the tax system. One Nation recently won its first lower-house seat in 30 years in the Farrer byelection, where its candidate took nearly 40% of the primary vote, and polls have shown the party running as high as 25% of the primary vote.

prop_args.thesis: Reforming housing tax breaks is a necessary correction that improves intergenerational fairness and reduces the economic grievance fueling populism.
mechanisms: First, the policy shifts demand away from speculative investors and toward owner-occupiers. This is because (1) negative gearing and capital gains concessions disproportionately reward people who already own assets, (2) those incentives inflate prices by making leveraged property investment more attractive, and (3) removing or narrowing them improves the odds that first-home buyers can compete on price.

Second, it restores legitimacy to the tax system by making it look less rigged for incumbents. Three reasons: one, younger renters see older cohorts receiving tax-favored wealth accumulation while they are locked out; two, that perception feeds the exact grievance politics One Nation exploits; three, visible reform signals that mainstream parties can still deliver fairness rather than leaving the field to anti-establishment actors.

Third, it can improve long-run economic efficiency by redirecting capital to more productive uses. This matters because housing speculation crowds out investment in business formation and labor mobility, while a less distorted tax system reduces deadweight losses and helps the economy respond to supply-side constraints rather than just inflating asset prices.

opp_args.thesis: Changing housing tax settings risks worsening affordability in the short term while punishing ordinary investors and creating new political backlash.
mechanisms: First, the reform may not materially lower prices if the core problem is supply, not tax treatment. One, Australia’s housing shortage is driven by planning constraints, construction bottlenecks, and population growth; two, investors may simply reprice or shift portfolios rather than exit the market; three, if supply does not respond quickly, renters and buyers still face high costs while the government takes the blame.

Second, it can hit middle-class households who rely on property as a retirement strategy. One, many investors are not the ultra-wealthy but older or leveraged households using property to build savings; two, reducing concessions can lower after-tax returns and create political resistance from a large constituency; three, that backlash can strengthen the same populist forces Labor is trying to contain.

Third, the policy may be fiscally and politically regressive if revenue gains are not targeted well. One, broad tax changes can be captured by general budget repair rather than housing assistance; two, if the proceeds are not directly recycled into social housing or income support, low-income households see little benefit; three, that leaves the most vulnerable still exposed to rent stress, meal skipping, and energy rationing.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether the budget can actually change housing access fast enough to matter politically. Prop wins if the key issue is legitimacy and grievance: even partial reform can signal fairness and undercut populist narratives, while Opp wins if structural supply constraints dominate and the tax changes mostly create pain for investors without fixing affordability.

cards.title: Syria Reopens Visa/Mastercard Access as EU Trade Normalisation Collides with US Sanctions
cards.background: On 12 May 2026, Syria authorised banks to work with Visa and Mastercard, a step aimed at restoring card payments and reconnecting the country to global finance. In parallel, the EU agreed to restore fuller trade ties with Damascus. Syria still seeks removal from the US state sponsors of terrorism list, meaning major restrictions from Washington remain in place even as Europe moves toward normalisation.

prop_args.thesis: Reintegrating Syria into global payment and trade systems is the fastest route to economic stabilisation and post-war reconstruction.
mechanisms: First, restoring card payments lowers transaction frictions and unlocks everyday commerce. This is because (1) households and firms can transact without relying on cash or informal hawala networks, (2) foreign visitors and diaspora remittances become easier to spend domestically, and (3) banks regain a basic interface with the formal economy, which increases liquidity circulation.

Second, EU trade normalisation creates a credible external demand shock that can revive productive sectors. Three reasons: one, exporters gain access to a larger market and better pricing signals, two, importers can source machinery and inputs more reliably, and three, the expectation of continued liberalisation encourages firms to invest rather than hoard capital.

Third, economic opening can strengthen state capacity and reduce conflict incentives. This matters because a functioning tax base, formal banking system, and employment growth give the government alternatives to predatory extraction, while ordinary Syrians become more dependent on peace and market stability than on wartime patronage networks.

opp_args.thesis: Partial economic normalisation will entrench authoritarianism and create dependency without delivering meaningful recovery.
mechanisms: First, opening finance and trade can funnel benefits to regime-linked elites rather than the broader population. One, banks and import licenses are easy to capture by politically connected actors, two, sanctions relief without governance reform rewards the same networks that profited under isolation, and three, concentrated gains can strengthen regime patronage rather than public welfare.

Second, the move may not solve the binding constraints on Syria's economy because US sanctions still block full reintegration. One, being on the US state sponsors of terrorism list deters global banks and insurers, two, firms will still fear secondary sanctions and compliance risk, and three, partial access can create the appearance of progress without enough capital inflows to rebuild infrastructure or employment at scale.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether limited economic opening is enough to generate broad-based recovery or merely enough to enrich connected insiders. Pro side wins if the judge prioritises immediate welfare gains and the compounding effects of normalisation; opposition wins if they show that US sanctions and elite capture make the reforms too shallow to change Syria's underlying political economy.

cards.title: Trump-Xi Summit Raises Risk of Tactical Detente or Escalating US-China Rivalry
cards.background: Bloomberg reports that US President Donald Trump is set to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday for a high-stakes summit. The article text provided is extremely limited, but it places the meeting in the context of broader US foreign policy tensions, with Trump also saying the US-Iran ceasefire was on "massive life support" after rejecting Tehran's latest peace offer. The summit is therefore being framed as a major bilateral encounter between the world's two largest powers at a moment of elevated geopolitical volatility.

prop_args.thesis: A Trump-Xi summit can reduce immediate great-power risk by creating a direct channel for crisis management and transactional de-escalation.
mechanisms: First, direct leader-to-leader diplomacy lowers miscalculation. This is because (1) it bypasses slow bureaucratic channels that often distort signals, (2) it allows both sides to trade concrete concessions on tariffs, export controls, or military deconfliction, and (3) it can produce a face-saving narrative that lets both governments step back without appearing weak.

Second, even a limited summit can stabilize markets and security expectations. Three reasons: one, firms and allies respond to the signal that escalation is being managed rather than left to drift; two, a temporary pause in punitive measures can reduce incentives for retaliatory spirals; three, clearer red lines around Taiwan, tech, or maritime incidents reduce the chance that a local flashpoint becomes a systemic confrontation.

Third, the biggest impact is that summitry preserves strategic optionality. This matters because a negotiated pause buys time for domestic adjustment on both sides, prevents immediate economic shock from tariffs or sanctions, and keeps open the possibility of a broader détente if both leaders find a mutually beneficial bargain.

opp_args.thesis: A Trump-Xi summit is more likely to entrench rivalry because it rewards coercive bargaining and produces only shallow, unstable deals.
mechanisms: First, summitry can legitimize brinkmanship. One, if both sides see that escalation forces a meeting, they have incentives to threaten more in the future; two, transactional deals are easy to reverse once domestic politics change; three, the absence of trust means any agreement is interpreted as tactical delay rather than genuine reconciliation.

Second, the structural conflict between the US and China is too deep for one meeting to solve. One, competition over technology, supply chains, and military primacy is zero-sum; two, both governments face domestic pressure to look tough, which limits concessions; three, partial deals can actually freeze in place a hostile status quo by giving leaders cover without addressing core disputes.

Third, the summit can increase instability if it raises expectations and then disappoints them. One, markets and allies may overread the meeting as a breakthrough; two, failure to deliver substantive outcomes can trigger sharper retaliation afterward; three, the optics of a summit can crowd out more durable multilateral containment or alliance coordination.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether the summit changes underlying incentives or merely manages optics. Prop wins if the round is about immediate crisis reduction and market stabilization; opp wins if the focus is on structural rivalry, because one meeting cannot erase the security dilemma or the domestic politics driving escalation.

cards.title: Bolivia’s Road Blockades Turn Economic Grievance Into Regime-Pressure Crisis
cards.background: On 12 May 2026, Bolivia saw widespread road blockades across major cities including La Paz and El Alto as protesters demanded the resignation of President Rodrigo Paz. The unrest is linked to fuel shortages, rising costs, and wage disputes. The blockades have disrupted travel and movement across key urban corridors, indicating a broader escalation from economic protest to political confrontation.

prop_args.thesis: The protests are a rational response to state failure, and forcing political accountability is the only way to break the cycle of shortages and inflation.
mechanisms: First, the blockades create immediate leverage over a government that has failed to solve basic supply problems. This is because (1) road networks are the main distribution channels for fuel and food in a landlocked, transport-dependent economy, (2) disruption in La Paz and El Alto directly raises the cost of inaction for the state, and (3) visible paralysis makes elite bargaining more urgent than slow institutional complaints.

Second, the unrest can force policy correction by making the political cost of mismanagement exceed the cost of reform. Three reasons: one, fuel shortages and rising costs are already broad-based and therefore politically salient; two, wage disputes mean the coalition against the government includes both consumers and workers, not just opposition activists; three, resignation pressure can reset negotiations if the incumbent is seen as incapable of restoring confidence.

Third, this matters because economic grievances become self-reinforcing when the state loses legitimacy. The longer shortages persist, the more households hoard, firms delay investment, and transport bottlenecks worsen, so a decisive political break can be the fastest route to restoring normal economic circulation.

opp_args.thesis: The blockades are counterproductive because they worsen shortages, hurt ordinary Bolivians first, and can destabilize the country without solving the underlying economic crisis.
mechanisms: First, the protests impose immediate social and economic costs on the same people they claim to defend. One, blocked roads interrupt fuel delivery and food supply chains, which raises prices further; two, workers and commuters in La Paz and El Alto bear the brunt of transport disruption; three, small businesses lose revenue faster than the government loses legitimacy.

Second, escalation can harden the state and reduce the chance of negotiated reform. One, a resignation demand narrows the government's room to compromise because it turns a policy dispute into a survival contest; two, prolonged unrest can justify repression or emergency measures; three, once violence and disruption dominate, moderate actors lose influence to more radical factions.

Third, the crisis may reflect structural economic constraints that protests cannot fix. One, fuel shortages and rising costs may stem from fiscal or import constraints rather than simple political will; two, wage disputes require budgetary trade-offs that street pressure cannot resolve sustainably; three, removing one president without addressing macroeconomic fragility risks repeating the same crisis under a new leader.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether coercive disruption is a necessary accountability tool or a self-defeating shock to an already fragile economy. Prop wins if they show the state is so unresponsive that only pressure changes incentives; opp wins if they prove the costs of blockade fall first on civilians and deepen the shortage cycle.

cards.title: Chinese Covert Influence Case Exposes Vulnerability of Local US Politics to Foreign Information Operations
cards.background: Eileen Wang, the mayor of Arcadia, a southern California city of about 54,000 people, resigned after the US Department of Justice announced she had agreed to plead guilty to a felony count of acting as an illegal foreign agent of China. Prosecutors say Wang and Yaoning 'Mike' Sun ran a website, US News Center, that posted pro-PRC propaganda and coordinated with Chinese officials through encrypted WeChat chats in 2021. The DOJ said Wang communicated with a PRC intelligence-linked figure, John Chen, and that the conduct occurred before she was sworn into office in December 2022; the city says no city funds, staff, or decision-making processes were involved.

prop_args.thesis: This case proves democracies need much stricter counter-foreign-influence rules because covert PRC operations can penetrate even low-level local office and then convert information access into political leverage.
mechanisms: First, foreign influence campaigns work best at the local level because one, local officials are less scrutinized than national politicians, two, they often control community trust networks and ethnic media ecosystems, and three, they can be cultivated cheaply through small-scale propaganda and social ties rather than overt bribery.

Second, the mechanism here is not just speech but covert coordination: one, Wang allegedly reposted pre-written PRC material within minutes, showing operational discipline rather than independent journalism; two, the use of a community-facing website let Beijing launder state messaging as local news; three, the hidden relationship meant voters and institutions could not evaluate conflicts of interest.

Third, stronger enforcement deters future penetration because one, foreign states rely on plausible deniability and low-cost agents, so prison terms and public exposure raise the expected cost of recruitment; two, disclosure rules and foreign-agent prosecutions create a paper trail that intelligence services can use to map networks; three, the broader signal is that public office in the US is not an accessible channel for foreign governments to normalize influence operations.

prop_args.thesis: The scandal justifies aggressive national-security screening and transparency requirements for elected officials and politically active media operators, even if that creates some burden on civil liberties.
mechanisms: First, the harm is institutional rather than merely individual because one, undisclosed foreign ties undermine voter consent, two, they can distort policy agendas through access and agenda-setting, and three, they erode trust in all local government by making legitimate officials look compromised.

Second, transparency rules are proportionate because one, the article shows the conduct was hidden, not merely controversial; two, the city itself confirmed the issue was not about municipal resources but about private conduct, so disclosure is the key safeguard; three, the state can target covert foreign direction without banning ordinary diaspora advocacy.

Third, this matters for democratic resilience because one, foreign influence campaigns exploit open societies' tolerance for speech and association, two, the cost of one successful covert agent can exceed the cost of many false positives, and three, public confidence in elections and local institutions is a strategic asset in great-power competition.

opp_args.thesis: This case is a narrow criminal matter about one individual's conduct, not evidence that local democracy is broadly compromised or that the US should expand surveillance and foreign-agent enforcement across the board.
mechanisms: First, the facts are limited in scope: one, the city said the conduct happened before Wang took office and no city finances, staff, or decision-making were involved; two, the alleged activity centered on a website and messaging, not on policy sabotage or classified access; three, the resignation shows existing accountability mechanisms already work when misconduct is exposed.

Second, overreaction creates civil-liberties and racial-profiling risks: one, broad 'China influence' crackdowns can chill Chinese-American political participation and journalism; two, vague foreign-agent standards can be weaponized against diaspora advocacy or dissenting speech; three, aggressive enforcement may conflate ethnicity with disloyalty, which itself damages democratic legitimacy.

Third, the strategic problem is better addressed through targeted intelligence and transparency, not maximal punishment: one, covert networks are best handled by focused counterintelligence rather than mass suspicion; two, the DOJ already secured guilty pleas and prison sentences for Chen and Sun, showing the system can punish real offenders; three, expanding the net too far can reduce cooperation from communities that are essential for detecting actual foreign interference.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is between isolated misconduct and systemic vulnerability. Prop wins if it proves covert foreign influence is cheap, scalable, and hard to detect in open societies; opp wins if it reframes this as a contained enforcement success where overbroad crackdowns would do more harm than the underlying threat.

cards.title: Trump Repeals Conservation Leasing to Restore Fossil Fuel and Timber Primacy on Federal Lands
cards.background: The Interior Department is отменing a 2024 Biden-era rule that made conservation an equal use of Bureau of Land Management (BLM) lands alongside drilling, logging, mining, and grazing. The BLM oversees about 10% of U.S. land and more than 1 million square miles of surface and subsurface resources, including coal and lithium reserves. The repeal takes effect 30 days after publication in the Federal Register and comes amid a broader Trump push to expand fossil fuel production and roll back renewable-energy support on federal lands.

prop_args.thesis: Repealing the conservation rule restores legal clarity and unlocks higher-value economic use of federal lands, which is the core purpose of a multiple-use land regime.
mechanisms: First, it reduces regulatory uncertainty for firms and land users. This is because (1) the Biden rule created a new conservation-leasing pathway that industry argued could block access to hundreds of thousands of acres, (2) the repeal signals that BLM lands will not be diverted into a novel 'non-use' regime, and (3) clearer rules lower permitting risk, which makes oil, gas, timber, mining, and grazing investment more likely.

Second, it improves allocative efficiency by prioritizing productive extraction over low-revenue preservation. Three reasons: one, federal lands are already designed under the 1976 Federal Lands Policy Management Act for 'multiple use,' not conservation primacy; two, conservation leases can crowd out activities with direct market value and tax revenue; three, the federal government can still protect land through other channels without distorting the BLM's leasing system.

Third, it supports domestic energy security and rural livelihoods. This matters because (1) the BLM controls major fossil fuel and mineral reserves, including coal and lithium, (2) western states depend heavily on grazing, drilling, and timber economies, and (3) expanding predictable access helps independent producers and ranchers invest, hire, and maintain output.

opp_args.thesis: The repeal entrenches short-term extraction at the expense of long-run public wealth, environmental resilience, and the government's duty to steward taxpayer-owned land.
mechanisms: First, it weakens conservation as a legitimate economic use of public assets. One, the Biden rule created a dedicated conservation program for the first time, allowing restoration leases just like drilling leases; two, removing it makes conservation structurally subordinate again; three, that means ecosystems that generate water, tourism, and climate value are underprovided because they lack a comparable leasing pathway.

Second, it increases externalized costs from environmental degradation. One, BLM lands include habitat and watersheds that support clean drinking water and endangered wildlife; two, extraction and grazing can leave landscapes damaged while corporations exit; three, without conservation leases and stronger oversight, taxpayers bear the cleanup and restoration burden later.

Third, it locks in a resource-curse style dependence on volatile extractive sectors. One, western states become more exposed to boom-bust commodity cycles; two, suppressing restoration and renewable-related land use slows diversification into higher-resilience land economies; three, that makes local communities more vulnerable when fossil fuel demand falls or regulation tightens.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether public lands should be judged by immediate market output or by total long-run social value. The opposition has the stronger structural case if the round is about stewardship and externalities, but proposition has an edge on institutional clarity and near-term economic predictability.

cards.title: US-Iran Ceasefire Collapses Into Coercive Bargaining Over War Termination Terms
cards.background: On 12 May 2026, Al Jazeera reported that US President Donald Trump said the Iran ceasefire was "on life support" after rejecting Tehran's latest proposal to end the conflict as "totally unacceptable." Iran's parliamentary speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said the US had "no alternative but to accept" Tehran's 14-point proposal, while Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said Washington had made "unreasonable demands." Iranian officials also warned they were ready to respond to "any aggression."

prop_args.thesis: Rejecting Iran's proposal strengthens deterrence and prevents a bad peace that would reward escalation.
mechanisms: First, it preserves bargaining leverage by refusing to normalize war termination on Tehran's terms. This is because (1) conceding now signals that military pressure can extract political recognition, (2) it encourages Iran to treat future crises as hostage-taking exercises, and (3) it weakens US credibility with allies who rely on Washington not to fold under coercion.

Second, it reduces the chance of a strategically unstable ceasefire. Three reasons: one, a rushed deal without enforcement mechanisms invites immediate violations and blame-shifting; two, it leaves core disputes unresolved, so both sides retain incentives to rearm and resume strikes; three, it can split the US domestic and allied coalition if the agreement is seen as capitulation.

Third, it creates space for a more durable settlement or a stronger coercive posture. This matters because a ceasefire that freezes an unfavorable balance can be worse than continued pressure: it lets the US demand verifiable concessions, keeps sanctions and military threats credible, and avoids locking in an Iranian victory narrative that would reverberate across the region.

opp_args.thesis: Accepting Iran's proposal is the least bad option because escalation risks a wider regional war and the US cannot force a better settlement at acceptable cost.
mechanisms: First, the military and economic costs of continued confrontation are likely to outstrip the gains from maximalist bargaining. One, renewed strikes risk retaliation against US forces, shipping, and regional partners; two, energy and trade disruption can quickly globalize the conflict; three, once casualties mount, domestic political pressure makes later compromise harder, not easier.

Second, Iran's proposal may be the only viable off-ramp because both sides are signaling exhaustion and escalation limits. One, Tehran is explicitly presenting a 14-point endgame, which suggests willingness to negotiate terms rather than fight indefinitely; two, Trump's own language that the ceasefire is 'on life support' shows fragility and the absence of a stable coercive equilibrium; three, rejecting the offer may collapse the channel entirely and leave only uncontrolled escalation.

Third, a ceasefire can be used as a platform for verification and future leverage. One, stopping the shooting reduces immediate civilian harm and creates monitoring opportunities; two, even a flawed deal can lock in de-escalation while diplomats work on inspections, sanctions relief, and sequencing; three, the US can always reimpose pressure later if Iran cheats, but it cannot easily undo a regional war once it starts.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether the US is buying leverage or buying time for escalation. Prop wins if you think conceding now entrenches coercive diplomacy and produces a fake peace; Opp wins if you think the immediate risk of regional spillover and uncontrollable retaliation outweighs the value of holding out for a better deal.
